name: Clérigos Church and Tower
short: Niccolò Nasoni's late-Baroque ensemble in the heart of Porto: a church, the brotherhood house and a celebrated 1763 bell tower roughly 76 metres tall.
long: The Clérigos Church and Tower are the masterpiece of the Italian architect Niccolò Nasoni, who came to Portugal from Malta in 1725. The ensemble brings together an oval-plan church, the brotherhood house and a slender granite bell tower 75.6 metres high. The tower did far more than ring: people set their clocks by it, it signalled ships on the Douro, and a flag hoisted there told merchants a steamer was approaching. Today it is one of the city's symbols and one of Porto's most visited viewpoints.
history:
The Brotherhood of the Clergy (Irmandade dos Clérigos) was founded in 1707, uniting three Portuense confraternities that cared for poor, sick and dying priests. At first it gathered in the Misericórdia church, and it soon became clear that it had outgrown borrowed rooms.

In 1731, under dean Jerónimo de Távora e Noronha, the design of a new church was commissioned from Niccolò Nasoni, a Tuscan who had reached Portugal by way of Malta and was then working on Porto Cathedral. The site at Cruz da Cassoa, next to the Adro dos Enforcados (the hanged men's yard), carried grim associations, but the need for a church of its own outweighed them. Construction ran from 1732 to 1749 with a pause in 1734–1745; the first Mass was held in 1748, though consecration came only in 1779, once the whole ensemble was finished.

Between 1753 and 1758 the brotherhood house was built, linking church and tower, and in 1753 Nasoni produced the design for the bell tower. Work went on from 1754 to 1763, ending with an iron cross on top and a statue of Saint Paul above the entrance. It was the tower, more than the church, that became Porto's landmark.

Beyond ringing the hours, the tower served the city: a daily gunpowder shot marked noon, it carried the commercial telegraph, its outline guided boatmen on the Douro, and a flag warned traders of an incoming steamer.

In 1910 the ensemble was declared a Portuguese national monument. A major restoration was completed in 2014 and honoured with the 2017 Europa Nostra award. In the church to which Nasoni devoted decades, his tomb is believed to lie.
facts: The tower is 75.6 metres tall (about 76 m), with 225 steps and six tiers.
The church was built in 1732–1749 and the tower in 1754–1763.
Its 49-bell carillon, bought in 1995, is among the largest in Portugal.
Nasoni won the commission in 1731, six years after arriving in Portugal.
The ensemble has been a national monument since 1910.
The 2014 restoration won the Europa Nostra award in 2017.
tip: Climb the tower at opening time, before 10 am, to beat the queue, and buy your ticket online. The stair is narrow and spiral, all 225 steps, so wear comfortable shoes. The view is best at sunset, when Porto and the Douro are lit up. The nearest metro is São Bento (line D), about a five-minute walk away.
